claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is controlled by the nanoscale interface architecture.
Compositional and structural heterogeneity at the interfaces promotes localized dislocation pile-up.
The starting films are nanoscale multilayers containing distinct FCC and BCC phases.
Changing layer thickness, interface coherency, or interfacial solute segregation alters dislocation interactions.
Interface heterogeneity and coherency mediate dislocation pile-up and subsequent interface sliding.
Dislocations accumulate at heterogeneous interfaces during sustained loading.
Less coherent interfaces allow accumulated dislocations to promote localized interface sliding more readily.
Localized interface sliding leads to progressive plastic deformation.
Tailoring interface quality changes the balance between dislocation pile-up and interface sliding and thereby changes creep response.
Interfaces engineered for enhanced coherency will reduce creep rate relative to the unmodified baseline.
Interfaces engineered for enhanced coherency will reduce localized interface sliding relative to the unmodified baseline.
Intentionally reducing interface coherency will accelerate creep relative to the baseline.
The proposed relationship is limited to sustained-creep conditions that preserve the nanoscale multilayer architecture.
Controlled annealing or interfacial doping can be used to enhance interface coherency in the tested multilayers.
